name: Shell of Light Falling in Anti-de Sitter Space
description: A shell of light, null dust, falling inward from the boundary of anti-de Sitter space and leaving a black hole behind it, Vaidya's metric with a negative cosmological constant. Viqar Husain wrote it in three dimensions in 1994, where the hole is that of Bañados, Teitelboim, and Zanelli, and in holography the collapse is the thermalization of the field theory on the boundary.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: A thin shell of light falls from the boundary of anti-de Sitter space toward its centre. Inside the shell and before it arrives the spacetime is anti-de Sitter space, and outside the shell and afterward it is a black hole [hubeny2007]. The event horizon of that hole forms at the centre before the shell reaches it [hubeny2007]. Viqar Husain wrote the metric for such light in three dimensions in April 1994, at the University of Alberta in Edmonton [husain1994]. Máximo Bañados, Claudio Teitelboim, and Jorge Zanelli had found two years earlier that gravity in three dimensions with a negative cosmological constant, $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$, has a black hole [banados1992]. Husain let the mass of that hole depend on the advanced time $v$, constant along each ingoing ray, $$ds^2 = -\left(\frac{r^2}{\ell^2} - m(v)\right)c^2dv^2 + 2c\,dv\,dr + r^2d\theta^2,$$ with $dm/dv$ proportional to the luminosity of the infalling light, and called it "the three dimensional analog of the Vaidya metric" [husain1994].¶With $m$ a positive constant $M$ the metric is the black hole of Bañados, Teitelboim, and Zanelli without rotation, whose horizon lies at $r = \ell\sqrt{M}$, and with $m = -1$ it is anti-de Sitter space [husain1994, banados1992]. While light falls in, the apparent horizon sits at $r = \ell\sqrt{m(v)}$ [husain1994]. Husain's subject was the inner horizon of a charged or spinning black hole, a surface where infalling radiation is infinitely blueshifted [husain1994]. Eric Poisson and Werner Israel had found in 1989 that the mass function inside a charged hole diverges there, and Amos Ori had modelled the divergence in 1991 with two Vaidya metrics joined along an outgoing shell of light [husain1994, poisson1989, ori1991inflation]. Husain built Ori's model from the metric of three dimensions and concluded that "mass inflation also occurs in three dimensions" [husain1994]. J. S. F. Chan, K. C. K. Chan, and Robert Mann extended the metric in June 1994 to a charged spinning hole whose angular momentum $j(v)$ grows with the light it absorbs, and found the mass function diverging inside a spinning hole as well [chan1996].¶José Lemos used the metric of four dimensions in 1999, where $\Lambda = -3/\ell^2$, $$ds^2 = -\left(1 + \frac{r^2}{\ell^2} - \frac{2Gm(v)}{c^2r}\right)c^2dv^2 + 2c\,dv\,dr + r^2d\Omega^2,$$ to test cosmic censorship, and gave its name as the Vaidya-anti-de Sitter metric [lemos1999]. Light whose mass grows from zero as $2Gm/c^3 = \lambda v$ with $\lambda \le 1/8$ makes a naked singularity at the centre, as it does with no cosmological constant [lemos1999]. With a flat front, whether a plane, a cylinder, or a torus, the same collapse makes a black hole and no naked singularity [lemos1999]. Andrew Chamblin, Andreas Karch, and Ali Nayeri took the metric of five dimensions in 2001 for the space on both sides of a universe that is a wall in anti-de Sitter space [chamblin2001]. The mass falling into the hole enters the wall's Friedmann equation as a term $2m/a^4$, with $a$ the scale factor, and scales like radiation [chamblin2001].¶In the correspondence between gravity in anti-de Sitter space and a field theory on its boundary, anti-de Sitter space is the vacuum of the field theory and a black hole is a thermal state [danielsson1999]. Ulf Danielsson, Esko Keski-Vakkuri, and Martín Kruczenski, in Uppsala, treated a collapsing shell in 1999 as a state of the field theory out of equilibrium that thermalizes as the black hole forms [danielsson1999]. Their shell was of slowly moving matter, and in the field theory they found unstable excitations, with masses set by the radius of the shell, which they named "shellons" [danielsson1999]. Kengo Maeda, Makoto Natsuume, and Takashi Okamura took Husain's shell of light in 2006, with anti-de Sitter space before it, and computed the boundary correlators of a scalar field on the hole it leaves [maeda2006]. Veronika Hubeny, Hong Liu, and Mukund Rangamani sent a shell of light into anti-de Sitter space of five dimensions later that year and showed that light rays crossing the interior put singularities into the boundary correlators, with a sharp feature when the event horizon forms [hubeny2007]. Hubeny, Rangamani, and Tadashi Takayanagi proposed in 2007 that the entanglement entropy of a boundary region is $k_Bc^3A/(4G\hbar)$, with $A$ the area of an extremal surface in the interior that ends on the region's edge and $G$ Newton's constant, and found in three dimensions that the entropy of an interval grows as the light falls in [hubeny2007covariant].¶Sayantani Bhattacharyya and Shiraz Minwalla sent a weak pulse of a massless scalar field in from the boundary in 2009 and found that it collapses to a black hole with a flat horizon, whose exterior "takes the Vaidya form at leading order in the source amplitude" [bhattacharyya2009]. Javier Abajo-Arrastia, João Aparício, and Esperanza López followed geodesics through the metric of three dimensions in 2010 and found that the entanglement entropy of an interval stops growing after about the time light takes to cross half of it [abajoarrastia2010]. They concluded that entanglement spreads through a conformal field theory of two dimensions at the speed of light [abajoarrastia2010]. Vijay Balasubramanian and nine coauthors treated field theories of $d = 2$, $3$, and $4$ dimensions in 2011, with the shell written as $$ds^2 = \frac{\ell^2}{z^2}\left[-\left(1 - m(v)z^d\right)c^2dv^2 - 2c\,dv\,dz + d\mathbf{x}^2\right],$$ where the boundary is at $z = 0$, and found that short distances thermalize before long ones [balasubramanian2011]. For matter at temperature $T$ they estimated a thermalization time of about $0.5\,\hbar/k_BT$, some $0.3$ fm/$c$ in a heavy ion collision [balasubramanian2011]. Hong Liu and S. Josephine Suh found in 2014 that after local equilibrium the entropy of a large region grows linearly, as if a wave swept inward from its edge at the speed of light for $d = 2$ and at $0.687$ and $0.620$ of it for $d = 3$ and $4$, and named the wave an "entanglement tsunami" [liu2014].¶Tarek Anous, Thomas Hartman, Antonin Rovai, and Julian Sonner built the shell inside a conformal field theory of two dimensions in 2016, from a ring of many local operators that each make one particle of null dust [anous2016]. At large central charge they reproduced the correlators and entanglement entropies of the earlier calculations on the metric of three dimensions [anous2016]. In that calculation a correlator decays exponentially for all time, which unitarity forbids, and they traced the loss of information to the terms they had dropped, exponentially small in the central charge [anous2016]. A. F. Cardona and C. Molina followed a free energy defined on the apparent horizon in five dimensions in 2026 and found that the black hole becomes the favoured thermal state once the horizon radius exceeds $\ell$ [cardona2026].

related.text: The hole the light leaves behind in three dimensions. With $m$ a positive constant the metric is this black hole without rotation, in ingoing coordinates [husain1994].
The hole the light leaves behind in four dimensions. With $m$ constant the metric is this black hole in ingoing coordinates [lemos1999].
The spacetime before the light arrives. It is the metric with $m = 0$ in four dimensions and with $m = -1$ in three [lemos1999, banados1992].
With a flat front and a constant mass the metric is the flat black hole of anti-de Sitter space, the black brane of holography [lemos1999, balasubramanian2011].
The same shell of light with no cosmological constant. As $\ell \to \infty$ the metric of four dimensions is Vaidya's ingoing metric [lemos1999].

The charged hole of four dimensions whose inner horizon two streams of light make singular. Viqar Husain wrote the metric of three dimensions to build the same model there, and found the mass function diverging too [husain1994].
Vaidya's metric with a positive cosmological constant, a radiating body in de Sitter space. Here the constant is negative and the light falls in.

A thin shell of dust with rest mass falling in flat space, with Schwarzschild's vacuum outside it. This shell is of light and falls in anti-de Sitter space, and in both the event horizon forms at the centre before the shell arrives [hubeny2007].

A ball of dust collapsing to a black hole in four dimensions with no cosmological constant. Here the matter is light, and the field theory on the boundary of anti-de Sitter space thermalizes as the hole forms [danielsson1999].

A universe that is a wall moving past the static black hole of anti-de Sitter space in five dimensions. Andrew Chamblin, Andreas Karch, and Ali Nayeri let light fall into that hole, and its growing mass is a radiation term in the wall's Friedmann equation [chamblin2001].
A shell of null particles lying on the horizon of the eternal black hole of three dimensions. Here the shell falls from the boundary into anti-de Sitter space and makes the hole [husain1994].

coordinates.name: Ingoing, Three Dimensions

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, with $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$
Mass function of advanced time, a pure number, with $m' \ge 0$ for infalling light; $m = -1$ is anti-de Sitter space and a positive constant is a black hole

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta)$, with the advanced time $v$ carrying dimensions of time and $2\pi r$ the circumference of the circle of radius $r$. The mass function $m(v)$ enters as $r^2/\ell^2 - m$, the coefficient of $-c^2dv^2$ [husain1994]. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cv$, a prime is $m' = dm/d(cv)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{v}$ means $d(cv)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Poincaré, Three Dimensions
domains: z = m^{-1/2} \;\text{(the apparent horizon, where } m > 0 \text{)}

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, with $\Lambda = -1/\ell^2$
Mass function of advanced time, an inverse area, with $m' \ge 0$ for infalling light; it is $1/\ell^2$ times the mass function of the ingoing chart

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, z, x)$, with the advanced time $v$ carrying dimensions of time and $z$ and $x$ lengths, where $z = \ell^2/r$ vanishes on the boundary and $r$ is the radius of the ingoing chart. The mass function $m(v)$ enters as the factor $1 - mz^2$ [balasubramanian2011]. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cv$, a prime is $m' = dm/d(cv)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{v}$ means $d(cv)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Ingoing, Four Dimensions

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, with $\Lambda = -3/\ell^2$
Mass function of advanced time, a mass, with $m' \ge 0$ for infalling light

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. The mass function $m(v)$ enters as $1 + r^2/\ell^2 - 2Gm/c^2r$, the coefficient of $-c^2dv^2$ [lemos1999]. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cv$, a prime is $m' = dm/d(cv)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{v}$ means $d(cv)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Flat Front, Four Dimensions

parameters.description: Anti-de Sitter radius, a length, with $\Lambda = -3/\ell^2$
Mass function of advanced time, a length, with $m' \ge 0$ for infalling light; a constant times the mass of a torus, the mass per unit length of a cylinder, or the mass per unit area of a plane

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, x, y)$, with the advanced time $v$ carrying dimensions of time, and $x$ and $y$ lengths along the front, which is a plane, or a cylinder or a torus where one or both of them are periodic. The mass function $m(v)$ enters as $r^2/\ell^2 - m/r$, the coefficient of $-c^2dv^2$ [lemos1999]. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cv$, a prime is $m' = dm/d(cv)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{v}$ means $d(cv)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, z, x, y)$, with the advanced time $v$ carrying dimensions of time and $z$, $x$, and $y$ lengths, where $z = \ell^2/r$ vanishes on the boundary and $r$ is the radius of the flat front chart. The mass function $m(v)$ enters as the factor $1 - mz^3$ [balasubramanian2011]. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cv$, a prime is $m' = dm/d(cv)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{v}$ means $d(cv)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(v, r, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, with the advanced time $v$ carrying dimensions of time, $r$ the areal radius, and $\chi$, $\theta$, and $\phi$ the angles of the 3-sphere. The mass function $m(v)$ enters as $1 + r^2/\ell^2 - m/r^2$, the coefficient of $-c^2dv^2$ [hubeny2007]. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cv$, a prime is $m' = dm/d(cv)$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{v}$ means $d(cv)/d\lambda$.
